Data augmentation methods employing word-to-word substitutions (SWTS) have effectively enhanced the translation capabilities of similar language pairs. However, the performance of SWTS in improving translation abilities for more challenging code-switched datasets remains unexplored. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by examining various SWTS strategies, including their adaptability to code-switched Arabic-English datasets of differing levels of difficulty. We also compare the outcomes of using SWTS with post-editing strategies that account for errors, and we evaluate and publish our code for reproducibility purposes. Key findings indicate that a carefully designed SWTS approach can effectively improve the performance of a translation model, but only for simpler and more complex datasets. Conversely, using SWTS on medium-level complex datasets yields lower results than employing no data augmentation strategy in these specific cases. We hypothesize that results of limited success in intermediate cases may be attributed to one of two issues: insufficient model robustness or inadequate SWTS design. Future research should focus on addressing these potential problems. We also provide a thorough explanation of our code-switching preprocessing method, intended to enhance understanding and stimulate the use of data augmentation in code-switched Arabic-English datasets. We are examining integrable membranes in a generalized lambda deformation of the classical M-theory and its double sine-Reed-Mermin version. For the lambda deformation, we discovered that the target space coordinates form an SU(2) invariant, resulting in two specific KdV systems. One KdV system is conventional, but the other includes novel components and higher odd derivatives. In the double sine-Reed-Mermin deformation, we found that the target space coordinates form a realization of the su(2|2) algebra, leading to two distinct deformation types. One type yields the well-known supersymmetric KdV system, while the other results in a new supersymmetric KdV system that includes odd derivatives. We provide specific soliton solutions for these systems. For the lambda deformation, we find soliton profiles for a conventional KdV system. For the double supersymmetric cases, we find soliton profiles for both the supersymmetric KdV system that includes odd derivatives and the newly introduced supersymmetric KdV system that includes odd derivatives. These profiles predict soliton interactions for all the systems under consideration. Moreover, we demonstrate that the double supersymmetric KdV system that includes odd derivatives exhibits superSU(2) Yangian symmetry. As a consequence, we are able to accurately calculate superlightcone correlation functions for the corresponding membrane worldvolumes. Furthermore, we are able to accurately calculate supercorrelation functions for the supersymmetric sigma model describing the membranes. By applying a similar procedure, we are also able to derive correlation functions for other systems that are closely related to the double supersymmetric KdV system that includes odd derivatives. These systems include a supersymmetric version of the non-Abelian T-dual of the defect lambda deformation and a double supersymmetric version of non-Abelian T-dual lambda deformation. In these two cases, we derive correlation functions for a 2d sigma model describing a superstring worldsheet. By comparing our results with established methods, we confirm that the derived correlation functions are consistent. In addition, we are able to accurately calculate correlation functions for a membrane interface crossing from a supersymmetric sigma model to a non-supersymmetric sigma model describing the related string worldsheet. These correlation functions exhibit symmetry under the superSU(2) Yangian algebra. As expected, we are able to recover supersymmetric correlation functions for the supersymmetric sigma model describing the membranes, while the mixed correlation functions exhibit a non-trivial dependence on the ratio of the string couplings. One of the primary issues in reinforcement learning is the assumption that states follow a continuity pattern in the environment's underlying structure. This assumption is crucial for developing useful value functions that can be utilized for decision-making. This paper introduces a novel form of continuity known as coarse-grained continuity, which is adaptable to various environments. Coarse-grained continuity is easily verifiable in many scenarios and can be treated as a defined theoretical characteristic. We have discovered a new algorithm, called QRCG, which leverages the assumption of coarse-grained continuity to improve off-policy correction. This method is the first to tackle the issue of Bellman errors in these complex environments. Under certain constraints, QRCG has been proven to converge to a consistent approximation of the optimal action-value function, even in the presence of disturbances. This algorithm's performance is demonstrated through theoretical analysis using an approximate dynamic programming framework. Furthermore, our experimental findings show that QRCG can effectively estimate action-value functions in intricate environments where traditional reinforcement learning methods struggle due to their dependency on fine-grained state continuity. This includes complex hierarchical and graph-based environments. Despite the absence of global connectivity in these environments, QRCG's ability to leverage local consistency and multi-start estimation allows it to achieve superior performance. These experimental results validate the practicality of our introduced concept of coarse-grained continuity. We introduce OASIS, a one-shot material identification network that can recognize any material at any viewing angle with just one example image. Traditional material classification techniques rely on collecting and labeling vast amounts of training data, which is impractical for real-world applications. To overcome this challenge, we've developed a novel approach using contrastive learning to train the network to distinguish between materials. By leveraging physics-based rendering, we can simulate real-world images of materials from sparse 3D models, enabling us to collect vast amounts of unsupervised data. OASIS identifies materials by comparing real-world images to artificially generated ones from a vast database, even when there are significant viewing angle changes. To our knowledge, this is the first one-shot material identification network capable of operating under rotation constraints. OASIS achieves state-of-the-art performance on both indoor and outdoor datasets, outperforming other techniques by a substantial margin, demonstrating its superiority with successful identifications of complex materials like wood and leaves. Furthermore, we've created an online platform where users can interactively identify unknown materials. The source code, 3D materials, and OASIS model are publicly available. A widely used technique for deriving the solar vector magnetic field from observations of two longitudinal components has been developed, yet the accuracy of its results remains uncertain. To gauge the potential for bias in this approach, a more straightforward model is introduced that assumes a two-arcsecond correlation between the longitudinal magnetic field and an azimuthal latitude-dependent function. This model enables the calculation of an estimated longitudinal transverse component. By comparing the coefficients from the proposed model to those from actual inversion techniques, researchers can identify the inherent bias, measured as the change in magnetic field strength, and associated spatial correlations. Furthermore, a method to mitigate bias is presented, simply by adjusting the coefficients using results from the more straightforward model. To verify the effectiveness of this approach, a simulation study is conducted, demonstrating that the inherent bias can be fully remedied. This method is also applied to observational data from NASA's Helioseismology Owens Valley Solar Array and a 2012 NASA Heliosphere ATST prototype, providing a reliable and reliable foundation for accurate solar data retrieval. The study of extremely old and rare celestial bodies called 'blue hook' stars offers significant insights into cosmic origins. These ancient stars retain precious elemental information from the early universe and are extremely infrequently born. Discovering and examining even a single blue hook star can yield valuable data, but identifying it poses a significant challenge. Researchers have developed an efficient method to locate blue hook and similar metal-poor stars by utilizing data from the Gaia satellite's spectroscopic database. In a recent experiment, this technique allowed for the identification of 509 metal-poor stars with surface temperatures below 6000 degrees Celsius and iron levels less than -3.0. Among these, 127 stars have temperatures below 5000 degrees Celsius and iron levels less than -5.0. We also discovered that our technique can retrieve known blue hook stars with high effectiveness, and thus holds the potential to discover previously unknown blue hook stars. This method can potentially identify up to 300 blue hook stars in the Gaia DR2 database, and we are currently analyzing these to discover new blue hook stars. In a preliminary look, the technique identified nine previously unrecognized blue hook candidates, and further verification is needed to confirm these discoveries. We are conducting follow-up observations to confirm the nature of these candidates, and these will be reported on in future research. In addition to blue hook stars, our technique identified 342 candidates with temperatures below 5000 degrees Celsius and iron levels less than -5.0, and we are conducting follow-up observations to verify their elemental information. These candidates may represent newly discovered extremely metal-poor stars, and we will report our findings when the verification is complete. We are also including all identified stars in the Gaia DR2 database in a supplementary table for easy access.

Continuous-phase modulation (CPM) is an attractive option for non-coherent communication systems due to its simple structure and the ease with which its symbols can be differentially encoded. Nevertheless, research has found that conventional differential detection of CPM often suffers from significant performance losses when the modulation index becomes small. In this study, an investigation into the reasons behind these performance losses has led to the discovery of an inherent assumption that may not be generally applicable. A critical analysis of this assumption has enabled the derivation of a precise expression for the error probability of CPM differential detection under any order of detection. This analysis has introduced an alternative method for calculating the system's probability of error. Moreover, a special case of this detection method has been found to outperform the conventional approach, even with only a single additional integration step beyond the conventional two integrations required for conventional differential detection. These modifications involve adding an additional integration step, an adjustment easily implemented with minor changes to existing receivers. This solution, derived through a combination of theoretical and numerical analysis, represents a major contribution to the field of communication theory, bringing this particular challenge to a close. Frustrated versions of the Toric code have drawn attention in the research community, characterized by periodic boundary conditions that hinder the emergence of topological order. Despite lacking topological order, these systems still exhibit notable numerical and analytical features, and are even capable of hosting a ground state with geometric properties on a lattice. A method involving a specific transformation of the Kitaev honeycomb model is detailed, which demonstrates the presence of this ground state within the model. Additionally, we outline approaches for accessing the ground state through various techniques and illustrate how degenerate zero-energy states, connected by lattice links, contribute to forming the ground state. A geometric framework is also proposed for characterizing anyons under a non-Abelian gapped phase, and it is shown that the ground state falls short of the criteria for hosting anyons. Lastly, we examine the expectations for boundary physics around a hole in the lattice and verify them against accurate numerical findings. To establish trust and ensure fairness, machine-learning models must be transparent and explainable.  Although numerous standards for algorithmic interpretability have been proposed, they lack a concrete quantifiable framework.  Thus, assessing whether a specific model meets the requirements of another has proven challenging.  In light of this obstacle, we developed a unique metric to gauge the comprehensibility of a model using a training approach inspired by human learning.  This approach trains basic neural networks with fixed parameters by feeding them input data and measuring comprehension based on how easily the networks generalize.  By leveraging this training method, we derived a cognitive complexity score for a variety of conventional datasets.  In addition, we established two benchmarks for algorithmic interpretability: the "human level" standard, matching the cognitive complexity of a human network, and the "minimal acceptability" standard, set at the average complexity of the top 75% of human networks in the corresponding space.  Our scores provide a quantifiable assessment of a model's understanding and can be used to evaluate whether it meets the "human level" and "minimal acceptability" standards.  In our study, we applied this score to several conventional datasets and discovered that some supervised models have achieved the "human level" on some benchmarks, while reaching the "minimal acceptability" standard proved significantly more accessible.  In our examination, we discovered that achieving transparency involves not only boosting a model's accuracy, but also carefully designing its architecture.  In conclusion, we believe that our scores, derived from a training method inspired by human learning, offer a valuable quantitative means of measuring algorithmic interpretability and evaluating the understanding of a model using a training approach informed by human cognitive capabilities.  In addition, we think that our research opens up fresh avenues for interpretability research, such as analyzing the architecture of a model and training methods that mirror human learning, in order to develop transparent models. The Steenrod algebra is a highly studied algebraic object in homological algebra and algebraic topology. As part of ongoing research on its cohomology, D. Stanke has already provided a detailed analysis of its cohomology groups across various characteristic sizes. In a subsequent paper, M. Bremke generated the cohomology groups in a more algorithmic manner and also extended the results to fractional coefficients. Building upon this work, we will refine Bremke's results by removing redundant components in the cohomology groups and further predict which components would appear in the cohomology groups of the subalgebra when operating on a finite number of modules. As a direct result, we will provide a compact version of Stanke's and Bremke's previous work, while also generalizing that work to the subalgebra's cohomology groups. In the process, we will introduce a novel concept, referred to as the critical height of a module, which serves to limit the complexity of the algebraic operations involved in the computation. As one of the technical challenges inherent in the prediction task, we will develop methods to identify the critical height for modules operated on by generators such as $\Pi^i$, $\Sigma^i$, or $\Theta^i$. Using these methods, we will provide evidence to suggest that the subalgebra's cohomology groups, when operating on a finite number of modules, tend to have fewer components than the general case, while also providing evidence to support a conjecture regarding the critical nature of the subalgebra's action on the module $\mathbb{Z}_{2^i}$. Concluding the research, we will provide several areas for potential future exploration. The research reported here was part of ongoing PhD research, conducted under the supervision of the author at the University of Münster. We also include the original thesis as an appendix. This paper establishes upper limits on the Hankel determinants for the $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(3)(\frac{1+wf}{1+wf_z})$ families, where $f$ and $z$ are analytic functions in the class $\mathcal{U}$ and $w$ is in the class $\mathbb{D}$, with $f(z)-f(\zeta)=z(1-\zeta)^2A$ for $0<|\zeta|<1$, and $A e^{r^2}> |w| e^{2|w_z|}$ for $|w_z|<|z|$. We also consider the general starlike class $\mathcal{S}$ and derive upper limits on the Hankel determinant for the function $\frac{1+wf}{1+wf_z}$ in that class. Our determinations outperform the existing upper limits by Miller in 1992, dry out previously established results by Liu in 2006, and replicate the findings of Wu in 2018. Furthermore, our analysis also reveals new findings for the class $\mathcal{U}$ and provides corrected results for the class $\mathcal{S}$, where the previous upper limits by Chen in 2017 were found wanting. The major methodological contribution of this paper lies in devising a new expression for $|H_2(3)(\frac{1+wf}{1+wf_z})|$ in terms of $|wf|, |wf_z|, |A|, |e^{r^2}|, |z|, |w|, |w_z|, |f(z)-f(\zeta)|$, which serves as the cornerstone for the determinations of this paper. Crowdsourced image datasets often contain diverse subjects like birds and insects, which can be challenging to classify accurately, especially when incomplete training data exists for novel or complex images. Model uncertainty, which reflects its confidence in the classification, can be utilized in conjunction with image entropy to determine the level of data uncertainty. Image entropy measures the dataset's uncertainty, while classification uncertainty corresponds to the model itself. A dataset consisting of birds and insects, which may resemble each other, is particularly suited to assessing data uncertainty through entropy measures. Models such as ResNet, which can be trained with noise, and PNN, which inherently produces output distributions, are well-positioned to estimate both model and data uncertainty. Combining multiple models, specifically PNN and ResNet, in an ensemble setting allows for the identification of data entropy and a bird/insect output distribution commonly referred to as 'human softmax.' Utilizing this approach, along with the advantages of temperature-scaled models and probabilistic neural networks, enables the reduction of classification errors resulting from incomplete training data by selecting the most probabilistically confident images for classification. Experimental results demonstrate that by employing this method on a bird/insect dataset with known output distributions, approximately 70% of the data set, or T=30, can be filtered out based on their entropy level, resulting in a 5% or lower margin of classification error. Furthermore, models trained with PNN output distributions produce minimal improvement in classification error, with reductions of up to 3%, suggesting that utilizing PNN output distributions as a training supervisory signal has some limitations. Through the analysis of the output distributions of each model, along with the calculated data entropy, it becomes clear that models producing a 'human softmax' output distribution, such as PNN and temperature-scaled ResNet models at T=30, demonstrate the most potential in identifying the most confident and data-rich images for classification. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for developing a robust, crowd-sourced dataset selection protocol, which can be widely applied to various classification problems involving complex, real-world images. Future research will focus on the automatic selection of the most confident and data-rich images from a much larger, real-world dataset consisting of thousands of unique images of coquina shells and abalone, which can be accurately classified with minimal classification error despite their visual similarities. A particular graph known as a covering array with strength two, and specified parameters k, n, and q, is defined by its nodes representing k-element combinations of a set containing q distinct elements. The edges connect the nodes whose corresponding combinations differ by at most two when compared modulo q. The minimum number of nodes required for this graph is represented by the symbol CA(k, n, q). Various bounds on the minimum number of nodes have been proposed in previous research. In this paper, specific examples of small covering arrays are provided to establish tighter bounds, specifically, CA(4, 27, 8) with 64 nodes, and CA(5, 243, 32) with 2432 nodes. These examples surpass the existing bounds up to a certain limit of k and q, and some of these nodes also constitute a substructure in larger covering arrays, specifically, CA(6, 729, 32). The research indicates that the existing covering array construction methods are ineffective in further reducing the size of these arrays when the parameters k and q increase. In fact, the methods are only able to guarantee a covering array with at most q + q/2 nodes for all possible parameters k and q. Consequently, new methods need to be developed in order to further reduce the size of these arrays beyond the existing limits, and towards achieving the proposed Hua-Hua bound, specifically, the minimum number of nodes representing the trinomial expansion of (1 + x + x^2)(1 + x^3 + x^6) in the field of integers modulo q. This bound would result in a particularly sparse array, specifically, an array of the type \begin{array}{cccc}x & x^3 & x^6 & x^7\end{array}, and this is why it is often referred to as the Hua-Hua bound. In this paper, the field of integers modulo q is replaced with the field of rational numbers, and specific cases are investigated where q equals a power of two, and particularly 8, and 32. The research also includes a discussion on the complexity associated with the covering array construction, and specifically, the time and memory required in order to efficiently construct an array with a large number of nodes using the brute-force method. This research investigates a particular class of quantum combinatorial problems in the form of nonlocal games, which involve perfectly correlated quantum states even when subjected to arbitrary local measurements and random noise. We prove that these games, when based on d-dimensional quantum systems, can be solved efficiently, a finding that directly implies the same efficiency for converting any such game into a classical constraint satisfaction problem on a line, known as the flow polynomial. This finding is further reinforced by the discovery that classical maximally correlated systems in the presence of random noise can also be efficiently solved, a conclusion that reflects a striking analogy between classical constraint satisfaction problems and nonlocal games. Domain adaptation has been extensively researched to handle distribution shifts.
The source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) variant, however, differs in that it
operates without access to data from the target domain. An SFDA method with
these constraints still aims to utilize target domain data for adaptation.
To address this challenge, we developed a novel adaptation technique called
Semi-Supervised Hypothesis Shift (SHS), which assumes that we can obtain a
target domain classifier without knowing the labels. An SFDA method using
this technique involves two main steps: first, we obtain a target domain classifier
along with a source domain classifier trained using different assumptions.
Next, we utilize the obtained classifiers in a semi-supervised manner to
generate pseudo-labels for the target domain, followed by training a transfer
model based on these pseudo-labels. By reusing the target domain classifier,
we can avoid needing target domain labels throughout the entire SFDA process.
The proposed SHS method is versatile and can be integrated with a range of
adaptation techniques. As such, we developed three specific SHS methods, known
as SHS-C, SHS-M, and SHS-L, representing instances of SFDA using label-free
target learning, instance-level label-free target learning, and class-level
label-free target learning, respectively. The SHS method is superior to other
SFDA methods, providing performance improvements of 11.8%, 13.9%, and 14.1% in
terms of accuracy for datasets including CIFARSDA, VLCS, and PFSD, and 3.2%
, 5.7%, and 5.5% in terms of accuracy for datasets including Office31,
Office100, and OfficeCFR. The entire implementation of SHS can be accessed at
https://github.com/uisrc/shs. As such, we successfully developed an SFDA
method with these constraints, yielding better results than other SFDA methods.

We evaluate the performance of recent methods for making broad inferences about multiple related variables, focusing on a new class of models where some variables may have outliers and others do not. We analyze how these methods can detect the need for a heavy-tailed assumption in some, but not all, variables, and we also investigate their ability to make reliable inferences for individual variables, particularly when some may have outliers. Our study primarily uses a key model for joint behavior of variables that includes both fixed and non-fixed components to test these methods. We find that a popular alternative to classical inference, such as using a square-root transformation, does not work well, but we also discover that another technique, such as using a square transformation, is not effective either. Through our investigation, we identify and implement a new class of models, referred to as the "trim-heavy-tailed linear model," that can make reliable inferences for variables with outliers as well as those without. We compare the performance of this model with others, including fixed-heavy-tailed, fixed-light-tailed, and model stripping approaches. Our results show that the trim-heavy-tailed model performs well in joint estimation and inference, and we find that it is able to accurately detect the need for heavy-tailed assumptions in some variables while ignoring them for others. An extensive numerical validation, as presented in the paper, demonstrates the efficacy of our reduced model in accurately predicting a variety of 2d vortex lattice evolution scenarios, thereby establishing the validity of our approach. Furthermore, an analysis of our model's properties reveals that it is both stable and Markovian in nature, thus allowing for a thorough probabilistic analysis of the positions, velocities, and widths of the vortices over time. An illustrative example highlighting the potential of our model in enabling a probabilistic analysis and risk assessment is also provided in the paper. Ultimately, the positions of the vortices over time are shown to converge to a stationary distribution, which we determine as the solution to a Poisson equation, which is used to inform the sampling strategy in the subsequent Monte Carlo simulations of our model. An additional, prominent Monte Carlo simulation result is also provided in the paper, which demonstrates the ability of our model to accurately predict the emergence of a self-sustaining vortex dynamics regime. A subsequent discussion of our model is presented in the appendix, which serves as a supplementary resource. Moreover, an additional numerical experiment is described in the appendix, which highlights the potential of our model in accurately capturing the transient behavior of our stochastic model following a sudden change in the input parameters. The concept of quantum entanglement extends beyond non-separability to include correlations in data, which can arise from various, potentially entangled, quantum states. In this work, we examine the complete state of a boson sampling device, characterized by mean photon source parameters such as mean photon number, visibility, and correlation metrics. We identify the correlation metrics $\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{m}}$ as a definitive indicator that these states are entangled. Specifically, for certain input modes, $\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{m}}$ serves as a Correlation of Entanglement (COE), while the full spectrum provides a fundamental measure of entanglement. Notably, our analysis reveals that the spectrum's structure is independent of the underlying quantum circuit, making COE a stable, experimentally consistent quantity. Furthermore, COE enables identification of the quantum circuit's type within a specified class, as well as identification of multipartite entanglement. Importantly, our results demonstrate that boson sampling device of a particular size can perform universal computational tasks, such as applying Sine-Wave Approximation, with current experimental capabilities, thereby validating plans for large-scale devices that are expected to elevate this capability. In addition to these results, our analytical framework facilitates derivation of maximum allowed visibility in boson sampling devices, offering insights into quantum noise and its relationship to photon number. Specifically, our study shows that non-Gaussian noise can be mitigated by adjusting the photon number, thereby enhancing visibility. Interestingly, our analysis also reveals that, beyond a certain threshold, further increases in visibility do not benefit large systems, indicating inherent trade-offs in boson sampling devices. The findings presented foster understanding of these devices' capabilities and guide their design, taking into account the intricate characteristics of entangled states in boson sampling devices. In various life science studies, researchers analyze temporal sequences to identify meaningful insights, but are hindered by the curse of dimensionality, causing feature space to expand exponentially with each additional data point. To overcome this limitation, a novel self-supervised method leverages domain knowledge to focus on critical dimensions from previous measurements when predicting future data points, thus enhancing regression performance using only a subset of relevant features. By integrating domain-specific understanding of temporal dimensions, this method effectively improves regression and anomaly detection capabilities on challenging, high-dimensional datasets like hyper spectral images and single-cell RNA sequencing profiles. Further analysis reveals that self-supervised learning enhances representation quality, and unsupervised feature selection streamlines the discovery of relevant features. Ultimately, this method accelerates the development of reliable, short-term prediction models in various life science applications. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengwengli/gsl. Using a synthetic dataset, we demonstrate the method's performance by comparing it to conventional supervised and deep learning techniques, such as SofTMN and Temporal CNN. Notably, at a 10% error rate, Guided Self-Supervised Learning achieves 91% of SofTMN's performance using 90% fewer features. When dealing with real datasets like CS1, HL60, and K562, our method produces effective prediction results, and at a 10% error rate, it surpasses SofTMN's performance by 30%, 20%, and 15%, respectively, while also reducing the required features by 80%, 70%, and 60%. To outperform SofTMN, the method utilizes domain-specific understanding of temporal dimensions to focus on critical features and introduces an unsupervised feature selection method to improve representation quality. As a result, Guided Self-Supervised Learning achieves state-of-the-art performance on challenging, high-dimensional datasets like HL60 and K562. Reinforcement learning strategies that do not rely on prior knowledge of the environment, such as learning from feedback alone, demand sophisticated approaches. When working within complex environments, several challenges arise: ensuring adequate exploration of the environment to learn its rules, and learning to predict and respond to the hidden states of the environment. Belief representation, which involves inferring the hidden states of the environment, is a key factor in many such situations. Past research has identified several methods for incorporating this factor into reinforcement learning strategies. This study evaluates multiple variants of a novel algorithm, Using Episodic Frequencies to Sample for Exploration (UEF-S), which addresses various aspects of learning in partially observable environments, including the incorporation of explicit belief representation and the efficient sampling of potential hidden states to facilitate exploration and data reduction. We then compare the results of this algorithm with those of existing methods, such as the power of recent algorithms in addressing partially observable environments, such as Soft Actor-Critic as an Generalized Matrix Bandit) and Generalized Value-Function Approximation for a corresponding increase in computational requirements. This study further extends its scope to a more complex problem, by adapting a widely used benchmark, the Hopper robot, to a fully observable and partially observable setting, to show that algorithms designed for the former type of problem can struggle to achieve good results in the latter, which highlights the need for tailored approaches in the latter scenario. This study further confirms this distinction by evaluating several existing algorithms, which, although capable of handling the former scenario efficiently, fall short in the latter case. Finally, multiple variants of a novel algorithm, Using Episodic Frequencies to Sample for Exploration with a belief, which addresses various aspects of learning in partially observable environments, including the incorporation of explicit belief representation and the efficient sampling of potential hidden states to learn and plan from the belief, are tested. Among these, only the algorithm, which assumes that the probability distribution of the hidden states, the probability distribution of the actions taken, and the probability distribution of the observations can be learned, was able to achieve good results in the Hopper benchmark in both settings, which highlights the significance of learning the hidden states of the environment to tackle the Hopper benchmark in both scenarios efficiently. This study's results indicate that there is a clear distinction between strategies for fully and partially observable environments, which highlights the need for further research in the latter case, which achieved good results by incorporating explicit belief representation and the efficient sampling of potential hidden states to learn and plan from the belief, which learned the hidden states of the environment

This paper addresses the challenge of action detection in videos, a task that depends on labeled video and spatial information. Given the labor-intensive process of labeling action and pose data, we propose a novel approach that employs graph convolutional networks to incorporate context from different spatial positions, and then utilizes performance-guaranteed action detection models. By combining our method with established techniques, we improve upon previous state-of-the-art action detection models, and demonstrate a significant increase in performance for both strongly-supervised and weakly-supervised action detection tasks, with the added benefit of reduced memory requirements. Experimental results show that our method achieves a 9.8% higher action detection top-1 accuracy than the previous best approach on THUMOS-13, using fewer parameters. Furthermore, on ActivityNet v1.3, our method outperforms previous action detection methods by 5.2% in top-1 accuracy, utilizing equivalent or reduced parameters. Our code and models can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/AllanZhu/abcnet. This research received partial funding from the NSFC (61976100). The associated video is available on the CVPR Insights platform.

The Image Similarity Challenge, held in 2021 as part of the RetiNet Week, aimed to evaluate readers' ability to accurately and consistently identify image tampering. This year's event introduced a new twist, an unexpected test on readers' domain generalization capabilities. We discovered significant disparities between readers of varying ages, expertise, and educational backgrounds, as well as a notable distinction between students with advanced degrees in art and those with other fields of study. It became apparent that readers who excelled in detecting manipulated images did so through different approaches. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the challenge's results, readers' performance variations, and the potential implications on forensic science. Through an analysis of an unsupervised clustering experiment, we identify distinct subgroups of readers sharing similar tendencies and present a new image authentication technique, involving the use of saliency maps, as an alternative to the widely accepted 12-point method. This research highlights the significance of conducting a thorough evaluation of readers' performance, revealing unique insights that can strengthen a forensic science based on human judgment. Ultimately, our findings suggest that human vision is not a reliable enough basis for image forensics and that a more nuanced understanding of the capabilities and limitations of human readers is essential. This knowledge can facilitate the development of more effective and reliable image forensic techniques. This study focuses on investigating the characteristics of nuclear matter at zero temperature within the influence of intense magnetic fields by employing the linked cluster variational method, which utilizes a cluster expansion of the many-body wave function with symmetrical slabs as the basic clusters. Utilizing this approach and considering the Fock-Bloch state for nucleons, we analyzed the ground state properties of nuclear matter in the presence of strong magnetic fields and its behavior as the magnetic intensity increases. Our findings show that the magnetic field impacts the interparticle distance, equivalent to one fermion radius, and the resulting compression leads to increased densities at a specific magnetic density, causing a magnetic-driven spin polarization that shows variations with magnetic intensity. Notably, our analysis reveals significant differences between our results and those obtained through other variational methods used to study mesoscopic systems, suggesting that the LoCV method offers an accurate microscopic description of matter behavior in extreme conditions, such as intense magnetic fields, where our approach demonstrates a magnetic-driven spin polarization that significantly surpasses previously reported results. Our research utilized a realistic nucleon-nucleon interaction, and we explored the impact of magnetic intensity on various ground state properties of nuclear matter, including density, coupling constant, spin polarization parameter, energy per nucleon, and saturation density, revealing interesting magnetic effects, such as increased spin polarization at a specific magnetic intensity, and the saturation density's response to magnetic fields. Our research contributes to understanding the behavior of dense matter in intense magnetic fields through a novel study, and we have made our calculations available for interpretation through a LoCV code implemented using Python. Our research explores the behavior of dense matter in intense magnetic fields, providing insights into atomic and magnetic structures, fusion processes, and various astrophysical phenomena associated with ultrastrong magnetic fields, such as neutron stars and quark stars, as well as quark-gluon plasma and other exotic states of matter and potential applications in materials science, including the development of superconductors and the description of magnetic effects in cold atoms and quantum fluids. Our research enables the exploration of novel magnetic and electronic properties, potentially influencing magnetic and electronic materials, as well as the behavior of dense matter, through external magnetic fields and_correlations. Our research offers new insights into atomic and magnetic structures, fusion processes, and various astrophysical phenomena, as well as the behavior of quantum fluids and superconductors. Our work has significant implications for materials science and astrophysics, as well as the behavior of quantum systems under intense magnetic fields. This can be difficult to determine, leading to a potential bias in the learned model. To mitigate this, various techniques such as data poisoning detection and protection, and secure real-time encryption, can be employed. In modern business environments, documents are frequently structured around tables which convey significant information, yet effectively retrieving relevant tables remains a persistent challenge. To address this issue, we developed a novel solution that combines graph neural networks, deep learning methods, and sparse tensor techniques to accurately identify and retrieve tables from vast document collections. Our approach involves converting tables into three-dimensional matrices and employing a learned representation mechanism, which leverages a vast index of table embeddings to pinpoint the most relevant tables based on their inherent content. Through extensive testing on diverse datasets, our method demonstrated a significant 10% to 50% or more performance boost in mean average precision (MAP) compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions, especially showcasing substantial gains on large datasets like the IRS2 collection. These improvements are particularly pronounced on large datasets like IRS2, where our method achieved notable gains of up to a 50% increase in MAP, surpassing state-of-the-art solutions. Empirical analysis revealed that our method excelled at identifying rare and unique table content while also maintaining a high capacity to detect tables with frequent patterns. Our method's exceptional performance is characterized by its ability to identify tables with rare patterns more effectively than those with frequent patterns, making it well-suited for real-world applications. Additionally, the method's code and other related assets are freely available on GitHub. The method's open-source implementation can be accessed on GitHub. Through our research, we made two significant contributions: (1) we developed a novel table retrieval technique that combines the strengths of graph neural networks, sparse techniques, and representation mechanisms, and (2) we identified effective strategies to accelerate the development and evaluation of such methods, which have the potential to revolutionize the field of information retrieval. Our research lays groundwork for accelerating the advancement of such methods in information retrieval, highlighting the importance of structured data, learned representations, and graph-based techniques. Ultimately, our research has far-reaching implications and encourages future investigations in information retrieval through structured data analysis. Our analysis suggests that future research should prioritize the exploration of more sophisticated graph neural networks, the development of more efficient indexing methods tailored to representation mechanisms, and the examination of structured data for retrieval. Our research provides valuable insights and sets the stage for future research in information retrieval through structured data analysis. This work extends the concept of cognitive complexity in decision-making models by incorporating a new layer. We investigate how different levels of cognitive sophistication interact within this framework, focusing on two-part agent structures. The first part makes straightforward decisions based on observable data, like a detailed map, while the second part uses more complex logic and imperfect information, such as a GPS navigation system. We analyze how partially informed low-cognitive agents defend themselves against low-cognitive and high-cognitive opponents, using a cognitive hierarchy of length two as our model. Our findings show that when facing less intelligent adversaries, informed agents can employ tactics like overestimating their opponents' knowledge to achieve better outcomes, but against more intelligent adversaries, this approach leads to suboptimal performance. In contrast, a two-layer cognitive hierarchy exhibits significantly greater stability, demonstrating a much lower impact when one layer is altered. We also prove the existence of a special type of cognitive hierarchy, known as the "cogwheel," where every possible length of the hierarchy maintains equilibrium against all less sophisticated opponents. The existence of this special hierarchy was previously unknown in 2-layer hierarchies, but our research reveals its presence, along with other important characteristics. Interestingly, high-cognitive sophistication does not guarantee success in this environment, but we found that the inverse relationship between the cogwheel and high cognitive sophistication provides a useful organizing principle. Finally, our study reveals a unique property of high-cognitive opponents, known as their "support set," which offers valuable insights into their behavior. We discovered a direct relationship between the cogwheel and a specific property of support sets, paving the way for future research on high-cognitive opponent behavior. Our findings suggest that even simple strategies can effectively coexist with more complex ones, and we can expect similar interactions at any depth of cognitive complexity, providing key insights for future investigation. The research further shows that high-cognitive opponents are characterized by distinct behaviors, and identifying the patterns of their support sets can help predict their actions, highlighting unique opportunities for successful strategies among those who think ahead. The research offers significant implications - simply being smart isn't enough, and being smart in the right way matters. The study's conclusions suggest that high-cognitive opponents are not automatically at an advantage, and being smart in a particular way can provide unique opportunities for successful strategies. The research further shows that high-cognitive opponents are not uniformly distributed in their thinking patterns, and their strategies vary greatly. The study's implications suggest that companies or individuals can effectively coexist with more complex or simpler competitors by identifying their patterns

Over the past ten years, substantial advancements have been made in the area of approximate membership query filters, specifically optimized variants of Bloom filters which enable fast probabilistic determination of set membership. While these improvements have reduced the number of potential false positives, they have not completely eliminated them. A new collection of algorithms, known as FOQ, is proposed in this work. This family of algorithms utilizes a combination of roll-ups and hash links to drastically minimize and ultimately eradicate false positives. In this study, the integration of both Bloom and FOQ is explored as a means to achieve a false positive free data exploration using previously constructed Bloom filters as a starting point. Several strategies for pairing these algorithms are discussed. This work examines three such pairing methods - by utilizing FOQ after Bloom, by alternating between Bloom and FOQ, and by utilizing FOQ before Bloom. This research computes the theoretical overhead required for achieving a zero false positive rate using these pairings. Furthermore, an assessment of the practical overhead incurred by these pairings is also conducted through experiments. The results indicate that by pairing FOQ with Bloom, a false positive rate of less than $10^{-9}$ can be attained with an overhead of approximately 9% in space. Additionally, by pairing FOQ with Bloom, a false positive rate of $10^{-12}$ can be attained with an overhead of $42\%$ in space. These pairings offer more than acceptable levels of practical overhead while providing the benefit of a completely false positive free exploration of the data. This work also highlights the value of FOQ as an independent tool for building a completely false positive free data exploration. This idea is further explored in the creation of a non-negative integer Bloom filter. This research further expands the scope of applications for both Bloom and FOQ, and the idea of combining these algorithms as a means to achieve a completely false positive free exploration of the data. This work also proposes a new algorithm, known as HFOQ, which integrates both Bloom and FOQ as a means to achieve a completely false positive free exploration of the data while minimizing the space required to do such a determination. This work offers a theoretical and practical assessment of the space required to achieve a completely false positive determination using HFOQ. This work also identifies areas of improvement for HFOQ, and the idea of integrating it as part of a larger lossy compression system, known as Kompress, to achieve a completely false positive free exploration of the data. A timely improvement in neural voice synthesis for control has been achieved, particularly in the area of pitch manipulation. The majority of existing voice models struggle to alter pitch without also affecting other aspects of the speech, making it difficult to produce high-quality recordings. Previous approaches have been unable to adequately address this issue due to the inherent relationships between pitch and other speech parameters. A new technique known as FastPitch addresses this limitation by utilizing a specific type of neural network called a phase reconstruction model, which is capable of independently manipulating pitch without requiring prior knowledge of speech statistics. While FastPitch represents an advancement in the field, it still falls short in certain aspects. To further enhance the controllability of pitch, we have developed an auxiliary training method called timbre-preserving pitch augmentation (TPPA). This algorithm intentionally distorts a voice model's pitch to create more significant and distinguishable pitch variations. By incorporating TPPA into FastPitch, we have seen significant improvements in its controllability. Notably, the resulting TPPA-FastPitch models exhibit more predictable and controllable pitch behavior, as well as increased robustness in situations where text-to-speech inputs become complex. Adding TPPA to other speech models would likely yield similar benefits in their controllability. To share these advancements with the community, we have created an open-source repository containing the associated code and auditory evaluations. This resource builds upon the existing research in this domain and is meant to facilitate future developments in the field of neural voice synthesis. Research into deep learning has highlighted several important issues related to the transferability of models. Various studies have investigated the factors that impact the performance of models when applied to different domains, and several methods have been developed to enhance model adaptability. While these studies provide valuable insights, they also make certain assumptions that may not always apply universally. For example, the conventional understanding of domain relationships is often treated as definitive, and the implications of model drift during deployment are frequently overlooked in favor of a static concept of model transferability. Further analysis is needed to deconstruct the assumptions underlying this research and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the role of domain agreements in model transferability. With this goal in mind, our work challenges two widely accepted agreements regarding model transferability, namely the consensus that label variability does not impact model performance and the notion that model drift does not impact domain transferability. By testing these agreements through experiments and theoretical analysis, our findings reveal significant implications for the design of models and their deployment. For instance, our findings suggest that incorporating transformations to address label variability can enhance model transferability. Furthermore, our experiments indicate that the performance of models is susceptible to drift, and that the extent of this susceptibility depends on factors such as model architecture, training data, and the characteristics of source and target domains. These findings have important implications for model design and deployment, and could be leveraged to improve the transferability of models. For example, our methods allow for the adaptation of pre-trained models, including LeNet5, ResNet18, and ViT-Base, to new domains while minimizing drift. While our methods do not guarantee optimal results, they provide a range of options for model transfer, and highlight the need for rigorous evaluation during model deployment. Ultimately, our work aims to advance the field of model transferability by challenging assumptions that may not be widely recognized as valid. By testing these agreements through theoretical analysis and experimental results, our findings provide valuable insights for the design and deployment of models. For instance, the implications of model drift are frequently overlooked, and our methods demonstrate that model transferability is highly dependent on model characteristics. These findings have significant implications for model design, and could be leveraged to improve the transferability of models. The management and scheduling of applications beyond traditional virtualization and containerization is becoming increasingly complex, necessitating more efficient approaches. A new universal container concept, called the Orchestration Container (orachestration.com), is being developed to simplify the deployment and management of workloads on cloud-based platforms. This paper introduces a container called Ozy, which embodies this concept, to enhance the user experience in using cloud-based resources. A comprehensive benchmark test was conducted to evaluate Ozy against containers and virtual machines in terms of performance, scalability, and power consumption. The results showed Ozy to be highly competitive in terms of performance and power efficiency, while demonstrating improved scalability and the ability to efficiently pause and resume operations compared to virtual machines. Furthermore, Ozy was found to be capable of executing tasks in half the time it took virtual machines, while using less power across various task durations. Additionally, a field study was performed to assess the performance of Ozy under real-world conditions, which confirmed its efficiency in handling tasks on large numbers of Ozy containers. In comparison to a cloud-based scheduling system, the study found Ozy to be capable of scheduling tasks 4.4-6.7% more efficiently than Amazon EC2. This research provides new insights into the benefits of using a universal container approach in scheduling and management applications. Our study reveals that Ozy is a viable container solution for deploying applications efficiently on cloud-based systems. A Python-based implementation of the Ozy concept, which is publicly available on GitHub, facilitated a hands-on evaluation of its performance and usability. This evaluation, which involved testing Ozy with a variety of tasks, showed that it is capable of achieving average performance and power efficiency comparable to that of Amazon EC2. A simulation study confirmed these findings and revealed Ozy to be 2.5-10.4% more energy-efficient than a cloud-based approach. In terms of performance, the study found Ozy to be 0-6.3% behind a cloud-based system. These results indicate that a universal container approach, such as the Orchestration Container concept, is a promising solution for improving the efficiency of application scheduling and management on cloud-based platforms. Our study not only compares the performance of different computing platforms, but also provides valuable insights into the benefits of a universal container solution, which can be applied to various fields of study. In addition to improving performance and power efficiency, the study's findings can also be applied to other areas, such as the efficiency of web search algorithms, which is an active area of research

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To tackle this challenge, we develop a mathematical optimization model representing the dial-a-ride problem in urban environments. Due to the model's complexity, we divide it into two manageable problems - a vehicle routing problem and a assignment problem - and introduce a set of cutting plane algorithms to enhance solution efficiency. Through computational experiments, we assess the effectiveness of the Branch-and-Cut algorithm in solving various urban dial-a-ride problem instances under real-world conditions. Furthermore, we compare our results with those obtained from two other approaches: a hybrid algorithm combining exact and heuristic methods, and a purely heuristic-based algorithm. The evaluation considers key performance indicators, including solution quality, computation time, and trip frequency. Our results demonstrate that the Branch-and-Cut algorithm excels in producing high-quality solutions, outperforming the other methods. Interestingly, the Branch-and-Cut method often finds solutions equal to or better than its hybrid and purely heuristic counterparts with significantly less computation time. While the hybrid algorithm may offer some computational advantages over the Branch-and-Cut method, our findings suggest that it generally falls short in terms of solution quality. Importantly, the Branch-and-Cut method has the potential to be faster than its hybrid and purely heuristic counterparts in real-world applications, where it consistently produces high-quality solutions in a relatively short amount of time. To further validate the performance of our approach, we conduct a sensitivity analysis to determine how various computational time limits impact solution quality. Our analysis reveals that the high-quality solutions obtained through the Branch-and-Cut method show considerable reductions when employing the hybrid algorithm. Ultimately, our results indicate that the Branch-and-Cut method stands as the top performer in solving urban dial-a-ride problem instances under real-world conditions. To facilitate future research, we provide detailed computational data, including problem instances, solution times, and solution quality for the various algorithms tested. Additionally, we make the Coq implementation of the Branch-and-Cut algorithm used in this study available to the public, enabling future researchers to build upon this work. As such, our approach may serve as a foundation for developing more advanced algorithms to solve urban dial-a-ride problem instances in the future. We developed an equation that describes the energy levels of S-conformal shadow matter, taking into account a particle's internal degrees of freedom and temperature effects. A few years ago, a new arithmetic encoding method was introduced, designed to simplify arithmetic operations in data compression. Following this innovation, several variants of this approach emerged, each tailored to specific characteristics of the encoded data. One such adaptation, referred to as Numbs, was specifically created to optimize numerical data compression, building upon the underlying principles of arithmetic encoding. Given its focus on numerical data, it was anticipated that Numbs would demonstrate exceptional performance in compressing datasets characterized by significant numerical patterns. Consequently, in this research paper, the Numbs algorithm is thoroughly evaluated using both synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing its performance alongside other leading compression methods, includingzip with LZ77 compression and subsequent encoding, fastBloom, FastBits, ELF, ELF-H, ELF-L, ELF-Lv, ELF rLLv, fastBOM, fastBOM+, fastBOM-L, fastBOM r, fastBOM-Lv, fastBOM z, fastBOM zr, fastBOM zrL, SNR, SNR-L, SNR r, SNR-Lv, SNZIP, SNZIP-L, SNZIP r, and SNZIP-Lv. It was observed that when data is heavily pattern-based, Numbs' performance is exceptional, with an impressive 99.95% achieving the highest possible compression rate. When data is randomly distributed and lacks notable patterns, Numbs' performance is comparable to other leading methods, with a slight superiority of 0.01% over the benchmark. Overall, the evaluation across multiple datasets and domains has consistently demonstrated Numbs' reliability and efficiency in real-world data compression. With continued advancements, this approach is expected to remain a prominent choice in both theoretical modeling and practical data compression applications. The dielectric properties of aqueous solutions, including those found in cement-based materials, play a significant role in understanding certain phenomena, such as freezing damage and polarization, that can influence a material's behavior. A comprehensive investigation into the dielectric behavior of pore solutions was conducted, using three different types of solutions - a simple system involving ions and nonelectrolytes, a more complex system comprising a multitude of ions, and a solution modeling the electrolyte concentration found in cement-based materials - to examine how ion combinations and concentration levels impact a material's dielectric behavior. Dielectric properties were measured over a broad frequency range, from 1 MHz to 10 GHz, and it was discovered that cement-based materials dielectric behavior falls within this range. A method for characterizing dielectric properties was developed and used; this method was applied to data from various solutions to better understand how dielectric behavior is influenced by the presence of water, temperature, and the concentration of ions, as well as to offer insights into the role that ion combinations play in dielectric behavior and how this might be applied to understanding certain phenomena, such as freezing damage. 
This research appeared in the journal Cement and Concrete Research under the title Dielectric characteristics of the pore solution in cement-based materials. Dielectric properties were measured over a wide frequency range - from 1 MHz to 10 GHz - and it was observed that dielectric behavior displays percolation, ion-combination, and Bruggeman effects. A simple model was developed to describe dielectric behavior as a function of concentration. It was discovered that dielectric behavior can be used to understand freezing damage through comparisons at low frequencies and concentrations, and at high frequencies and concentrations it was observed that dielectric behavior can be used to estimate the amount of electrolyte present. This research showed that dielectric behavior and electrolyte concentration are related to certain cement-based materials phenomena.

This study examines the relationship between different measures of complexity in a Boltzmann machine model. By employing information-theoretic measures, we explore how these measures correlate with each other, as well as how they respond to variations in the model's architecture and parameters. Our results suggest that certain information-theoretic measures of complexity are equivalent, while others reveal distinct characteristics of the system. Furthermore, we investigate how these measures of complexity reflect the significant structural changes that occur in the system when hidden units are introduced. Using a detailed case study, we assess the effectiveness of these measures of complexity as indicators of phase transitions within Boltzmann machine systems. Our empirical analysis indicates that different information-theoretic measures of complexity may predict different types of transitions, including changes in hidden unit activity and correlation patterns. Overall, we demonstrate that multiple information-theoretic measures of complexity provide valuable insights into the system's behavior and suggest that a multifaceted approach to complexity analysis is most effective. These findings contribute to the understanding of the role of hidden units in Boltzmann machine models and have potential implications for the design of future neural network architectures with hidden units. They may also inspire new information-theoretic measures of complexity that capture additional aspects of the system. The study aims to assess the potential of ensembling neural networks on a challenging task, specifically identifying various white blood cell types from microscopic image captions. Initially, agents collect and compile a vast dataset of ImageNet and Google Open Datasets containing 25 types of white blood cells without captions. Following this, a neural network model is trained to analyze captions and assign a specific label to each image. To enhance the model's accuracy, agent teams train and average their respective neural network models, achieving significant improvements. Notably, the unified model exhibits confidence in its predictions and securely processes images online, outperforming the individual models and matching the performance of top ensembling models. Moreover, we examine the model's sensitivity to caption variations, its robustness to divergent image labels, and its ability to handle rare cell types. Our analysis indicates that even rare cell types can be identified to some extent, and the model's predictions become more accurate with increasing rare cell counts. Additionally, incorporating more captions into the dataset enhances the model's performance. Our study indicates that the unified model is capable of identifying the correct cell type to a high degree, specifically 95.0% for neutrophils, 85.7% for lymphocytes, 85.2% for monocytes, 83.3% for eosinophils, and 82.1% for basophils. We also discover that the unified model is highly consistent, with a standard deviation of 0.095 for neutrophils, 0.086 for lymphocytes, 0.085 for monocytes, 0.083 for eosinophils, and 0.081 for basophils. Our analysis shows that the unified model outperforms its individual counterparts in nearly all cases, demonstrating its potential to efficiently classify and accurately identify rare and uncommon white blood cell types. Our findings indicate that the unified model exhibits exceptional generalizability, confidence, and reliability, making it well-suited for practical applications in medical settings. Importantly, our research highlights the capabilities of ensembling neural networks in medical microscopy, a relatively underexplored area of study. Our study provides valuable insights into the practical implications of ensembling neural networks in medical microscopy, offering opportunities for future research to address potential limitations of the current study. Our analysis indicates that the unified model's exceptional generalization capabilities could potentially be replicated for other challenging classification tasks, making ensembling a valuable technique for achieving robust classification results. Our study provides essential practical insights into the success of ensembling neural networks in medical microscopy

The utilization of pre-trained language models has become the standard approach for numerous NLP applications. However, their reliance on substantial supervision, which is often costly and demanding, has not received the same level of attention. This paper aims to rectify this by proposing an unsupervised and low-data supervision method for analyzing the internal knowledge and abilities within pre-trained language models. By leveraging cluster analysis on outputs generated from diverse inputs, we successfully extract prominent features, which in turn enable us to determine the models' capacity for understanding surface language and developing new concepts. Furthermore, we establish a new framework for uncovering the knowledge embedded in language models through self-supervised learning. By employing this method and introducing a novel evaluation criterion, we are able to assess and compare various models' knowledge content across multiple benchmarks. Interestingly, our experiments reveal that BERT models contain substantial knowledge of geographical and societal understanding, while ELMo models possess knowledge related to emotional concepts. Moreover, our unsupervised approach yields comparable results on several semantic tasks as those obtained from supervised learning, and our method outperforms several models in understanding word meanings. Finally, our method demonstrates the ability to analyze BERT models' knowledge of word meanings and multiply it through transfer learning with minimal supervision, which in turn results in exceptional performance on several benchmarks. Interestingly, our method also identifies considerable biases present in the embedded knowledge of these language models. This research was made possible by the computational resources and data provided by the 'Service Algorithme en Machine Learning' of the fundamental research platform 'SwissDataScienceHub'. The code and data used in this research are publicly available at the provided repository. Future research could involve developing more advanced methods for analyzing the knowledge and abilities within language models and uncovering and addressing the various forms of bias present in their embedded knowledge. Additionally, we could further investigate and develop the knowledge content and understanding of social and geographical understanding within language models and apply this method to the analysis and development of multimodal language models and the detection of bias in their embedded knowledge. By employing this method and data, we are able to identify and address several forms of bias present in the embedded knowledge of language models, which in turn may lead to unfair AI predictions in certain contexts. This research reveals that BERT models contain substantial geographical knowledge. The embedded knowledge of BERT models also demonstrates an evident bias, which may lead to unfair predictions in certain contexts. This research highlights the importance of analyzing the knowledge content and embedded abilities within language models through our method and provides valuable insights for its design and development. Most popular kernel functions assume that samples are drawn from the same distribution, which does not always match real-world scenarios where samples come from different or varying distributions. This draw distribution is often referred to as the support of the kernel function. Aims to propose a draw distribution that is universally suitable for a wide range of high-dimensional datasets, while being flexible enough to process samples from different distributions. 

We start by recognizing that standard kernel functions can be viewed as functions derived from the maximum-likelihood estimated distribution of a single data point. This implies that choosing an optimal draw distribution involves balancing between a large enough set of distributions to cover all possible data distributions, and the lower-bounded likelihood of this distribution to prevent overfitting.

We propose a draw distribution based on the Gaussian tangent space and our approach, dubbed Non-Exchangeable Tangent Kernels. We begin by examining the relationship between neural networks and distributions, and then develop a method for creating kernels from neural networks. We demonstrate that kernels derived from neural networks are versatile and can be used to cover a wide range of distributions. We also illustrate that NTK kernels are highly efficient and can process a significantly larger number of data samples compared to traditional kernel functions.

We test the efficiency of NTK kernels by replacing multi-kernel functions with a single NTK kernel function in various machine learning tasks, replacing traditional kernel functions. Our results show that NTK kernels outperform kernel functions in several important areas, such as multi-task learning and using a small amount of data to simulate a large amount of data. 

We extend NTK kernels to support multi-task learning. Our approach involves developing a neural network that can represent various draw distributions. The stability of non-Hermitian topological phase is generally impacted by correlations between systems' fermions. Within a solvable model of interacting fermions on a ring connected to an environment that decays, our analysis shows that time-evolved density profiles can indicate whether a topological state has shifted to a lower energy state due to environment interactions or if it remains in a lower sublattice state. In cases of weak interactions, our results reveal that fermions' density distributions narrow as they approach equilibrium, while for strong interactions, our findings show that density profiles in topological states and their degenerate counterparts converge at two distinct $k$-values characteristic of each state, signifying that the topological state remains in a lower sublattice state. Furthermore, by calculating the local von Neumann entropy (LNE), our analysis identifies correlations between fermions on neighboring sites as the primary driver of LNE, which increases as $t^2$ before reaching its maximum at an intermediate time $t_t$, leading to a quasi-stationary state where LNE is independent of time. For strong interactions, our analysis shows that the LNE is maximum in topological states and their degenerate counterparts, indicating that the topological state remains in a lower sublattice state. By calculating the local spin entanglement (LS) on neighboring sites, our analysis reveals that the topological state remains in a lower sublattice state by binding adjacent lattice sites together. We examine how neural networks can be applied efficiently to the keyphrase spotting task, which entails identifying crucial phrases within a sentence for understanding its significance. We evaluate several models, including CNN, LSTM, GRU, Transformer-based architectures, and various combinations of these elements. Considering that IoT devices may not have sufficient computational resources, we also investigate the use of lightweight models, such as those originally designed for image analysis (eXtrNet, MobileNet), to determine their effectiveness in keyphrase spotting. Our experiments involve testing the models on the Hyperlink dataset across three different scenarios to simulate growing computational constraints and observe how the models change as the task becomes more demanding. Our results show that a model combining elements of the Transformer architecture and lightweight models performs exceptionally well, achieving an 83.0% precision and 83.0% recall, while being significantly lighter and using fewer parameters than the most accurate model in our study. Ultimately, we discover that models optimized for image-related tasks can efficiently handle keyphrase spotting, making them suitable for deployment on IoT devices despite requiring only a small fraction of the processing power. Notably, our most efficient model requires only 55.6% of the processing power and 75.4% of the memory of the most accurate model in our study, yet still achieves nearly identical performance. Our study's code and models are publicly accessible.

We explore a dimer model on an octahedral lattice with non-trivial coordination and define an interaction that causes it to exhibit a critical behaviour. By mapping this model to a two-dimensional Yang-Mills theory with massless Dirac fermions in a background gauge field, we establish the existence of this critical behaviour. Our proof stems from the emergence of a massless, non-zero flavour of Dirac fermions within this background gauge field. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this behaviour's key characteristics align with those of the dimer model and other related systems of Dirac fermions in distinct lattices. Building on an idea first proposed by Polyakov, we show that by representing dimers as polyhedra and changing the dimer model's interaction, it's possible to access and analyse dimer configurations and various Dirac fermion systems within a common framework. This approach, known as dimers' geometric unification, enables us to study dimer configurations and Dirac fermion systems using identical methods. As an example, we resolve a dimer system on a square lattice with a critical behaviour for the first time without relying on cluster expansion techniques. Our analysis also reveals the dimer configuration density for the octahedral lattice and an alternative geometric method for introducing critical behaviour into a dimer model on a square lattice. Furthermore, we outline the broader significance of these findings for statistical physics and Dirac fermion systems in general. Using Polyakov's idea, we develop a geometric approach to non-perturbative two-dimensional gauge theory and Dirac fermion systems. Our findings indicate that non-trivial dimers experience a critical behaviour and contribute to the broader dimer system family. They also represent two-dimensional fermions within an associated Yang-Mills framework, linking dimers to Yang-Mills in both dimer geometry and interaction terms. Lastly, we explore the connection between dimer configurations, Yang-Mills, and quantum gravity through Polyakov's idea. This connection allows us to study dimer configurations and two-dimensional, massless Dirac fermions within an associated background gauge field with common methods. Our analysis reveals that dimer configurations and Dirac fermions represent distinct facets of the same broader dimer system family. They share a common geometric approach and can be expressed through identical dimer models. Our approach to these systems, rooted in Polyakov's idea, offers a unified and unified understanding of these systems, linking them to Yang-Mills and quantum gravity.
