A recently established metric called "adversarial susceptibility" measures how prone machine learning models are to being compromised by slight alterations in input data, resulting in incorrect outputs, even with minimal loss in performance on typical evaluation metrics. In this study, the concept is extended to evaluate self-supervised speech models. Experiments were conducted on two datasets, Speech Commands V2 and LibriSpeech, utilizing six distinct network architectures, including models pre-trained on raw speech data, those fine-tuned on annotated data, and self-supervised models. Results indicate that self-supervised models are particularly vulnerable to adversarial modifications, while being relatively resistant to noise and capable of generalizing across different datasets and speech types. It's hypothesized that self-supervised models are more susceptible to being compromised because they rely on speech statistics that can be easily manipulated, whereas other models perform better after being fine-tuned on annotated data. This study also shows that self-supervised models are more resistant to being altered randomly, suggesting that their retraining on speech statistics can provide some protection against unstructured modifications, but not necessarily against more targeted and subtle changes to the input data. Ultimately, it's recommended that the concept of adversarial susceptibility be applied to a broader range of speech-related models in the future. This collaborative effort is aimed at establishing a cutting-edge dilution refrigerator test bed to assess its functionality in a wide range of applications before deploying it in IBM's in-house research and development facility. Identifying and categorizing online content as hate speech is a critical task with deep social implications. Researchers have developed models utilizing natural language processing techniques, often employing a class imbalance technique due to the skewed distribution of hate speech data. This study presents an integrated framework, consisting of various feature selection and class weighting methods, to classify hate speech. We also compare the performance of different machine learning algorithms using datasets annotated as hate/offensive vs. non-hate/neutral content and vs. derogatory vs. non-derogatory content. Evaluations are conducted on two datasets, known as Dehate and Twitter, using six classifiers and six feature selection methods, in combination with different class weightings. F1-score and accuracy metrics are employed to analyze the results, ultimately demonstrating that support vector machine and logistic regression perform better on the two datasets, specifically identifying hate/derogatory vs. non-hate/neutral content and hate/derogatory vs. hate/non-derogatory content, respectively. We also identify the top-ranked features influencing classification on the two datasets and discuss their implications in detail. Furthermore, this study contributes to the field by analyzing the impact of different class weighting schemes on performance and offers expert advice on choosing suitable techniques. We also explore the applicability of various natural language processing approaches and discuss the limitations and potential biases of the used datasets. Ultimately, the goal is to apply these models to a broader range of text classification problems. We plan to utilize these models to automatically classify and detect various forms of toxic language, including hate speech, offensiveness, bullying, and derogatory content, as well as identify other types of abusive language. A landmark survey in this field since 2015, this work identifies areas in need of further research and highlights the key attributes of the collected datasets, including their size, the period in which they were scanned, and the level of ground truth available for training and evaluation. A standardized evaluation protocol is presented, along with a discussion of the strategies used to acquire and prepare the datasets, including the process of removing irrelevant content. Additionally, the survey explores the essential qualities of documents presented in a page-level format, as well as the intricate nature of the task of providing an automatic table of contents in underdeveloped countries where access to education is a significant challenge. Ultimately, the survey provides crucial insights into the most effective approaches to the analysis of the datasets and suggests the development of new collections that can bridge the existing gaps in the field. These datasets can be found online at https://github.com/isa-group5/HMSIDatasets. A video summarizing the survey is available at https://youtu.be/4QrjwvX9O9g. The extensive benefits of deep neural network (DNN) based medical image analysis have been acknowledged, with their applications ranging from disease diagnosis to treatment. However, these models are highly susceptible to errors caused by misleading image labels due to the limitations of manual verification. Although it's economically viable to improve these labels, the sheer volume of images necessitates a more efficient solution. Current methods often adapt models to account for errors, but directly correcting the noisy labels can be straightforward. We introduce the label rejuvenation mechanism (LRM), a novel approach that assigns greater trust to correct class labels for images, while reducing the reliance on potentially erroneous labels. We enhance LRM with a Bayesian statistics driven mechanism, using the distribution of image predictions to determine the most credible class label. The efficacy of our proposed approach is evaluated against state-of-the-art methods and a standard image classification model, utilizing the well-known LabelNoise and Backward pass for forward sampling (BILS) dataset to compare performance. The results indicate that our method surpasses LRM by 2%, while surpassing the baseline model trained with clean data by 5% and matching or outperforming the current top method, BILS, which trains the model with noisy data under a distribution matching objective. The code for our method is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/vikasiraj/BayesLRM to enable immediate testing and evaluation. The findings of our study indicate that our mechanism effectively corrects image labels, reducing reliance on misleading information and the economically challenging label improvement method. The research also showcases the value of the Bayesian statistics in guiding the label correction process, resulting in label rejuvenation. The goal of the out-of-category (OOC) challenge was to assess the ability of classification models to detect their own limitations. In this context, models were trained on data from a specific distribution, typically referred to as the "within-category" or training set. Once trained, they were tested on data from a different distribution, often referred to as the "out-of-category" or testing set. Various experiments were performed to evaluate how different types of models, such as neural networks and distance-based methods, as well as traditional and deep learning approaches, behave in out-of-category scenarios. In one experiment, models were tested on data from a different distribution, but with the same number of features, as the within-category data. In another, data was tested with a different number of features than the within-category. Additionally, some experiments used within-category data with randomly masked features to mimic the effect of a different feature setup in a more subtle way. Our analysis of these experiments reveals a significant performance gap between models and distance-based methods, suggesting the need for further research in out-of-category challenges. Key takeaways from the analysis include recommendations for both the research community and practitioners. While the specific domain of the challenge limits its direct application, the underlying insights remain relevant and should guide future research. Several potential ways to enhance the challenge and obtain more insightful results are proposed, such as working with multi-modal data and incorporating more than one OOC distribution. Additionally, it is recommended that models be designed not only to perform well within their trained domain but also to recognize and efficiently handle out-of-category data. Ultimately, the ideal model should be one that performs well across various scenarios and data configurations. The paper's findings and recommendations should inspire the research community to tackle the out-of-category challenge in innovative ways. This research investigates geodesic distances between points on the Gaussian random field manifold. The analysis reveals that these distances are calculable and efficiently approximated through summing geodesic distances between adjacent points, with each increment being maximally achieved in the underlying field's domain. To facilitate these calculations, a geometric representation of the manifold's structure is developed, enabling its visualization through a two-dimensional embedding. Furthermore, the research introduces a novel, rapidly computable test for determining whether a given embedding is valid. By applying the tools developed here, the research explores the geometric structure of various canonical manifolds, including those generated by independent Gaussian random variables, Gaussian distributions in high dimensions, and stochastic partial differential equation ground states. It also demonstrates how to use geodesic distances for assessing model fit and identifying optimal models among a set of candidates. Ultimately, the research applies these methods to analyze relationships between adjacent cells in the body's immune tissue. Specifically, the tools enable efficient identification of cell clusters characterized by distinct, homogenous patterns of gene expression. The research' findings are corroborated by a clustering approach using hierarchical thresholds, thus validating the geometric model's utility in understanding complex high-dimensional data. By incorporating sparse grid construction, the proposed sparse-grid adapted spectral Koopman method can work effectively with problems featuring multi-dimensional parameter spaces, without increasing computational demands. This is achieved by utilizing the tensor product structure of sparse grid bases, which can be treated as traditional Koopman equation parameters, thus enabling the use of existing time-dependent approaches developed for these equations. Our research explores the computational benefits of the proposed sparse-grid adapted spectral Koopman method, showcasing its accuracy and efficiency in estimating the Koopman operator and its eigenvalues for several complex examples. These examples feature flows created using laminar and turbulent Navier-Stokes equations with diverse boundary conditions, as well as multi-variate perturbations to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in identifying non-linear dynamical systems. Overall, the results illustrate that the sparse-grid adapted spectral Koopman method is a powerful tool for identifying multi-variate flow patterns and their underlying linear and non-linear correlations, even in cases where the underlying dynamics are complex. Moreover, the proposed method is remarkably simple to implement, requiring only the substitution of standard basis functions with sparse grid ones in existing time-dependent approaches for solving the Koopman equations. As a consequence, the proposed sparse-grid adapted spectral Koopman method serves as a highly efficient tool for identifying multi-variate and non-linear flow patterns, and it is particularly well-suited for use in computational frameworks such as those employed in the Reduced Order Models and surrogate modeling of fluid flows. Ultimately, the proposed method is expected to be highly valuable in a wide range of applications, including multi-variate flow identification, reduced order modeling, surrogate modeling and the exploration of sparse grid constructions for other modeling and simulation challenges. A computational software framework written in the TensorFlow language has been developed to implement the proposed sparse-grid adapted spectral Koopman method, and it is available upon request. In probabilistic learning, organisms often face a dilemma between maximizing their rewards and accurately predicting the likelihood of future rewards. While some individuals adopt an optimal strategy known as probability matching, others choose suboptimal methods, such as maximizing the number of rewards, with varying degrees of skill exhibit different levels of both tactics. A key neural region involved in learning is the midbrain, particularly the substantia nigra pars compacta, which encodes the difference between predicted and actual rewards. We investigated the relationship between learning approaches and brain responses to surprise. We discovered a correlation between areas responsive to prediction errors and people's inclination towards optimal as opposed to suboptimal learning strategies. Although probability matching strategists showed uniform activity in response to errors, those who learned suboptimal strategies displayed distinct neural responses across multiple trials, indicating varied brain responses to surprise, such as differences in the intensity of their responses, locations where they process the surprise, and what parts of their brain are involved. These results suggest that skill levels in learning may influence how accurately they assess the likelihood of future events, a concept known as subjective probability. Moreover, we observed that probability matching strategists showed more consistent subjective probabilities than suboptimal strategists, consistent with optimal learning being associated with accurate assessments of uncertainty. Overall, our findings indicate that areas responsible for learning may influence an individual's likelihood of adopting accurate or inaccurate learning strategies, with varying brain responses to surprise in suboptimal learners. These diverse brain responses among suboptimal learners may represent distinct learning mechanisms or brain adaptations. As a result, our study suggests that tailored interventions designed to improve learning strategies may be more effective for individuals with similar brain adaptations, indicating that brain responses may serve as an essential indicator for guiding personalized learning programs. Furthermore, our study highlights the significance of suboptimal learning tactics as a distinct learning strategy and its potential mechanisms and brain adaptations. Importantly, our study offers valuable insights into the distinct learning pathways of suboptimal and optimal learners, particularly how their brains process the difference between predicted and actual events, which may contribute to the development of multiple distinct learning theories. Moreover, our study offers insights into the potential mechanisms and brain adaptations of suboptimal learning tactics, which may help to bridge the gap between theoretical learning models and brain-based learning approaches. Ultimately, our study highlights the importance of considering various learning strategies, such as probability matching, maximizing rewards, and accurate assessments of uncertainty, and their distinct brain mechanisms. We developed a method for creating new interactions between humans and robots by using a combination of machine learning and simulations. This approach lets non-technical people teach robots new behaviors by providing a set of steps that the robot should take in a sequence of actions. We designed an interface that makes it easy for people to input their own instructions for how to interact with environments that contain objects and activities not typically found in computer models. For mobile robots to safely operate in unknown and unfamiliar settings, effective navigation and mapping capabilities are crucial. Conventional mapping techniques often rely on prior knowledge or experience to organize spatial information, yet they may falter when encountering unfamiliar layouts. To address this limitation, a novel navigation approach called HiTMap is introduced, which employs a hierarchical diagram representation to encode topological information about unfamiliar environments. By representing the layout as interconnected nodes and paths, and using a directed graph to calculate probabilities and determine the best course of action, HiTMap enables robots to adaptively navigate unknown spaces. In a simulation testing the navigation skills of robots using this new map compared to traditional mapping techniques, the results revealed that HiTMap demonstrated superior performance, with the robot taking 20% fewer steps and reducing its time in unfamiliar areas by 25.5%. This significant improvement makes HiTMap a more efficient and effective tool for navigating unknown environments. Furthermore, the representation's simplicity and universality make it an ideal solution for a wide range of robotics navigation challenges. To facilitate the adoption of HiTMap in real-world applications, a step-by-step guide is provided for robot practitioners to integrate this new map in their systems. By using HiTMap, mobile robots can successfully navigate through unfamiliar settings with increased speed and efficiency. Computed Tomography (CT) is an essential imaging technique with a broad range of applications across medical and industrial fields, but it often has image quality compromised due to signal loss, noise, and speckles caused by sensor imperfections and data constraints. To address these limitations, we propose an advanced reconstruction model that integrates methods for estimating x-ray flux, sensor denoising, and identifying different material types. By formulating a task-oriented transfer function and adjusting its spectral mixture, we can determine the material's x-ray attenuation coefficients. To clean up sensor noise and improve image resolution, our model also uses a refined version of the Zeyde et al.'s model, incorporating task-oriented denoising filters and clean image estimates. To evaluate the performance of our proposed framework, we create a comprehensive numerical test suite that simulates various noise levels, signal strengths, and material combinations. To support future advancements in CT technology, we also use our test suite to investigate potential enhancements, such as higher signal strength and more noise-resistant performance, suggesting our method can serve as a starting point for next-generation CT imaging systems. In information retrieval, search queries often include one or more questions along with a context, aiming to provide a relevant response by identifying key entities within that context. For instance, a user might ask "Who sings 'Stairway to Heaven'? What label does this song belong to?" to find relevant entities within a musical context. The task of retrieving entities based on context is known as Contextual Entity Retrieval (CER). One challenge in CER is that not every entity in the context is important, and only entities directly related to the query's context should be considered. To address this, we present Term Relevance Response (TRR), an approach designed to pinpoint contextually important entities by considering questions and their context. We propose generating an entity list along with a question-specific context, and training models based on pre-existing data to improve our method. We also develop a new dataset called Question-Stacy, which represents one of the few available CER datasets, to evaluate TRR. By comparing our method against other approaches, we find that TRR produces a significant improvement in retrieval accuracy, outperforming other methods by at least 1.5% in the Question-Stacy dataset. We also compare our method against other approaches for ranking entities and find that TRR produces a substantial enhancement in retrieval accuracy, outperforming other methods by at least 1.5% in the Question-Stacy dataset. The new Question-Stacy dataset and our Term Relevance Response method are available at https://github.com/kuhzi/TRR. In this research, we employ Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to analyze EHRs, using the GNN to build a patient similarity graph based on the patients' EHR graphs. This study addresses the issue of maximizing energy efficiency in wireless networks that use relay stations, especially in scenarios where relay usage is optional. We optimize energy efficiency by combining power allocation and scheduling in a single approach, focusing on a given transmission time and a specified source-destination pair. Our proposed technique involves optimizing energy efficiency through network coding, resulting in significant energy savings with full diversity and a high data transfer rate. We demonstrate, however, that implementing this method in all possible combinations of scheduling and power allocation would lead to an excessively complex problem. To resolve this issue, we develop two approximate optimization methods - one conservative and one aggressive - which ensure that scheduled and power-allocated transmissions are aligned. We test these methods using various network configurations and show that they offer efficient solutions, with the aggressive method providing better energy savings in networks with a high density of relay stations. Furthermore, we illustrate how to use our approach as a baseline for finding optimal solutions. Additionally, we show that our method, though designed for a given time slot, can be easily adapted for use across multiple time slots, enabling full system optimization. We compare the performance of our method with a range of benchmarks, including a global optimum, and illustrate how it can be used to achieve efficient energy savings in a variety of network configurations, resulting in better performance than direct scheduling and power allocation methods. We also show that one-better and two-better approximations provide improved energy savings of 1% and 1.5% respectively, while linear programming yields a 1.2% improvement. We result in substantial energy savings of up to 86% and 85% for 20 and 25 nodes respectively, resulting in considerable performance enhancement over the best available methods. We observe similar improvements in scenarios that combine scheduling and power allocation, resulting in energy savings of up to 83%. These results suggest the value of exploring joint scheduling and power allocation techniques that take into account relay station diversity to achieve better performance, while indicating the adequacy of using a single time slot to model a high degree of parallelism, allowing for a reduced computational complexity in large-scale networks. A thorough examination of X-ray absorption near edge spectra (XANES) at high fluence reveals a nonlinear process influenced by the accumulation of excess electrons within the material. To model this nonlinearity at the atomistic level, we introduce the concept of electron groups, each exhibiting unified absorption and excess charge. The rate of charging these electron groups governs the overall absorption near the edge, thus simulating the observed nonlinear XANES. This model provides a starting point for developing microscopic explanations of high-fluence spectra, potentially leading to the recovery of near-edge linear absorption. We have computed reference spectra both without and with excess charge in order to highlight the key factors contributing to the nonlinearity. Additionally, parameters for simulating various reference spectra have been included in the model, enabling the investigation of how linear XANES absorbs non-linearly under high fluence conditions. The model is accessible in the open-source Python code, Sharpen, and is available for further use. Future research will involve adjusting the rate parameters to fit experimental data and then utilizing these parameters to elucidate the underlying electron dynamics during high-fluence XANES experiments. Research has shown that high-fluence XANES dynamics primarily involves the sequential unshelling of outermost electron orbitals. We hypothesize that outer electrons are generated first when the fluence is low, and that further investigation at higher fluences should uncover a more intricate electron dynamics, where inner electrons are generated in conjunction with outer electrons. This is in line with theoretical predictions of electron-generated excitations, and with further analysis at high fluence and energy resolutions, it may be possible to quantify the degree of excitations at each electron orbit simultaneously. This could provide insights into fundamental questions regarding the generation of excess electrons and excitations during high-fluence XANES, ultimately yielding a deeper understanding of the physics behind these processes. We anticipate that our model and analysis will contribute to a more detailed and experimentally-informed model of high-fluence XANES, and the model code and research are available for further development. Furthermore, our model and analysis may be extended to other nonlinear spectroscopies, such as Raman, near-infrared, and second harmonic generation, and the model may be applied to other fields such as biology, chemistry, and materials science to investigate nonlinear spectral responses to varying fluence and radiation intensities. We anticipate that our model and analysis may be used to shed light on the generation of excess electrons and excitations during high-fluence XANES

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions plays a vital role in diagnosing and treating the disease. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of multiple MS segmentation methods. However, these techniques are often hospital and population-specific, requiring new training from existing datasets for use in other hospitals. This population shift can be costly and time-consuming, prompting the question of whether existing models can be adapted through continued learning to include new populations. We investigated this issue by initially comparing the performance of a pre-trained, deep learning-based MS segmentation model against a model trained exclusively on our own hospital's data. This led to the observation that a pre-trained model may underperform due to data inconsistencies. We then introduced the concept of "data-robust continuation learning," allowing the model to adapt to new populations while maintaining its original performance. This involved adjusting the loss function to account for subtle differences in the new dataset. Our findings indicated that continuing learning with our hospital's data did not compromise the model's ability to identify MS lesions, showing results comparable to a model trained exclusively on our own data, while significantly reducing the need for additional annotations. This concept was further validated through experiments mimicking the distribution of our hospital's data. We also performed comprehensive ablation studies to identify the most effective configuration for practical implementation. This research marks the first examination of adapting existing population-specific MS segmentation models to accommodate new populations, offering a cost-effective solution to expanding the reach of these models without requiring additional annotations. Furthermore, we introduced a novel approach to configuring the continued learning process for efficient results. This research was facilitated by a new dataset comprising MRI scans and annotated MS lesions from our own hospital, as well as code and data made publicly available. This research has the potential to significantly reduce the time, effort, and resources required to fine-tune models for new datasets, accelerating advancements in the field. Additionally, it facilitates the development of more resilient and adaptable training methods, capable of overcoming changes in data distribution. This has the potential to benefit a broader range of image segmentation challenges. While the primary focus of this research was MS lesion segmentation, the underlying principles can be applied to a wide array of segmentation tasks, underscoring the importance of data distribution in the continued learning process and the need to account for these differences through adjustable training objectives. This research has the potential to significantly enhance the continued learning paradigm, paving the way for the development of population-agnostic models capable of sustained adaptation, thereby facilitating a seamless and efficient transfer of models across different populations, including hospitals, laboratories, and research organizations,

This intuitive measure, easy to interpret and calculate, requires minimal information about a signal or image, and its mathematical properties have been extensively studied.  This work discusses the connections between the bipolar contrast and other measures of contrast, investigates its practical uses, and demonstrates its sensitivity to changes in signals or images at different scales. By assuming limited data anomalies, small errors in model accuracy, and quasi-periodic patterns in these errors, our approach leverages a deep learning network to identify mistake patterns in the model. Our method can be integrated with any decoder based on attention and demonstrated on three language pairs showing an improvement in consistency. Additionally, it results in enhanced coherence and overall translation quality when combined with existing optimization techniques. In this research, we investigate the specific issue of finding English writing experts among MTurk workers. To address this problem, we first assessed the quality of MTurk workers by posting a series of writing-related tasks, which revealed a significant disparity in the skills of top-rated workers. Subsequently, we developed and implemented a targeted recruitment strategy focused on attracting high-quality workers who possess writing expertise, utilizing a customized job posting and selection process. The results of our study indicate that by targeting qualified workers through a strategic recruitment approach, MTurk-based projects can successfully attract and retain a skilled workforce, ultimately leading to successful outcomes. Text clip retrieval, a critical component of many modern systems, is becoming increasingly important due to significant advancements in breaking down text into compact yet informative segments, and then using these segments for efficient comparison. Current top-ranking models typically employ a multi-modal encoder that breaks down both text and clips into fixed-size tokens, followed by a comparison process that relies on a cosine similarity metric. Notwithstanding significant progress made so far, there are significant drawbacks associated with the widespread adoption of such multi-modal encoders, primarily due to difficulties in accurately capturing relationships between tokens and their global context. In order to overcome these limitations, we introduce TS2-Net, a cutting-edge text-clip retrieval model that effectively captures relationships between tokens and their surrounding environment. TS2-Net achieves this by token movement and selection mechanism that facilitates an adaptive comparison process. Our extensive evaluations with a diverse range of data sets, including AVA, DiDeMo, ALBUM, and CLIP-VID, have consistently shown that TS2-Net surpasses the retrieval capabilities of various state-of-the-art models, and we make our related source code and training data sets publicly available. We introduce a new method for training deep neural networks to tackle sparsity
issues effectively. Our approach employs a simple yet efficient cost function
that minimizes the difference between a network's output and a target value at
specific training data points. This cost function is formulated as a network
input vector's movement to a sparsely distributed set of points. The movement
is achieved by adding a variable amount to each point. Our objective is to have
most of the movement mitigated over time, resulting in a network input vector
that approximates a minimal set of points. A dual formulation of this problem
involves finding a vector configuration and weight that encourage movement,
with both vectors starting as approximations of a target value. The key factor
here is identifying which data points should be moved and which ones should remain
in their original position. By introducing a dual variable indicating which
points should move, we can identify key features that must be maintained during
the movement. The movement of points is then determined by input data, and we
can backtrace to find the optimal network input configuration. The key benefit of
our approach is that we can achieve sparsity in a broad network architecture,
including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Our method has been verified to
be effective in various CNN models and is also shown to be applicable in other

In modern network systems, entities are connected in complex, dynamic structures known as evolving graphs. These graphs experience gradual transformations over time due to internal or external influences. Understanding and analyzing such graphs requires specialized approaches that incorporate both spatial relationships between entities and temporal changes. Various domains rely on evolving graph applications, such as social media, road networks, bike-sharing systems, protein interactions, and multi-layered data combinations. Graph evolution can result from diverse processes, including entity appearances, disappearances, and updates, relationships added or removed, and isolated subgraphs. To effectively study these graph transformations, researchers have developed multiple embedding frameworks that capture a graph's overall structure in low-dimensional space while preserving its network properties. This work surveys existing evolving graph representations, categorized by space, time, and relationship focus. Additionally, we provide recommendations for future research directions and outline key challenges and limitations in this area. The accompanying code can be accessed via https://github.com/chenxu1992/Evolving-Graph-Embedding. Our work also draws inspiration from embedding methods for temporal networks, diffusion graphs, multi-layered graphs, and temporal node classification. However, we delve deeper into evolving graph representation research, exploring the advantages of incorporating graph evolution and key challenges that distinguish our work from general graph embedding research. This survey aims to promote dialogue within the NLP and data mining communities and stimulate innovative developments in evolving graph representation research. Finally, we highlight various benchmark datasets for evolving graph embedding research. Our work is the first comprehensive survey in this area, covering both static and evolving graph embeddings, distinct from survey recommendations (de Cao et al., 2020) and data papers (Perram et al., 2020), and offering insightful discussions on embedding methods. Following the survey recommendations by Deng and Li (2019) and Shang et al. (2017), we identify promising research areas and future challenges. This work also expands upon a survey on temporal graph embeddings by Li et al. (2020), exploring the more focused area of evolving graph representations. The primary distinctions between our work and graph embedding surveys lie in their scope and the specificity of the target problem. This work also draws upon multiple survey recommendations and data papers in the graph embedding domain. The accompanying code for our work is included at https://github.com/chenxu1992/Evolving-Graph-Embedding. When working with robotic arms equipped with cameras attached to the end of a tool or a sensor, accurately positioning the camera is crucial for effective observation. Traditionally, robots use movement planners or pre-programmed steps to adjust the camera based on specific tasks, but these methods are often time-consuming and fail to consider the broader context. With the presence of an assistant or experienced operator, robots can receive guidance on where to position the camera, providing an alternative approach. Our research focuses on robots working alongside human operators in controlled environments, using computer vision techniques to analyze images taken by the cameras and generate adjustments, learning these adjustments from human input through deep neural networks, such as MIXNET. Additionally, we developed a new representation for camera movements that accounts for objects in the scene, enabling more accurate and robust predictions when operating in new environments, even without further fine-tuning. During experiments, we discovered that our robots often preferred to follow established paths and efficient routes, indicating a preference for learned behaviors that reflected scene-specific patterns rather than pure image content. Our mixed-Planner approach, built on this mixture of human and automated planning methods, successfully navigates, demonstrating stronger performance than automated or fully human-controlled methods in independently operating robots. This work was initially published in 2020 under the title 'Mixed-Planner: Unsupervised Learning of Eye-in-Hand Camera Trajectories using a Single Image'. In reverse reinforcement learning (RRL), we address the problem of
automatically generating a policy that mimics a teacher's behaviors, observed during interactions in an unfamiliar environment.  The teacher's actions, observed at discrete time points, include a reward assessment for each state, providing insight into desired behavior.  Our objective is to develop a policy compatible with these reward assessments within the constraints of an existing policy transfer system.  We will achieve this through the following key contributions:  First, we will use the teacher's reward assessments to create a representation of the desired state space, built on a variable size vector observation system.  Secondly, we will demonstrate that our RRL framework can be treated as a non-smooth convex optimization problem.  Thirdly, we will show that our algorithm, based on an exploratory gradient descent method, is both efficient and reliable, reaching an optimal solution in a relatively short time, at most equivalent to the number of steps taken by the teacher.  Fourthly, we will verify our algorithm's performance in a real-world scenario, with actual experiments conducted.  Furthermore, our algorithm is highly adaptable, easily incorporated into existing algorithms, including supervised learning and reinforcement learning methods, as well as other algorithms requiring a policy transfer system, without needing significant alterations. The field of network analysis is rapidly expanding with numerous applications across various sciences, significantly contributing to our comprehension of complex systems. Research on weighted networks has grown particularly substantial, enabling in-depth exploration of properties that the simple use of counts or binary values cannot reveal. Since it's impossible to measure every node in every network, it's essential to have established methods for handling missing data. We propose that weighted network analysis should incorporate two key specifications: defining the direction and strength of edge weights. We discuss how Weighted Grouping Methods can effectively incorporate missing data by assuming it follows a similar distribution as existing network weights. We examined the performance of six weighted grouping methods on various synthetic and real-world networks. Notably, our analysis highlights the need for additional information about the data collection process for drawing statistically valid comparisons. We also provide a benchmarking tool to help evaluate the effectiveness of grouping methods in real-world applications. Together, these findings should aid researchers in choosing appropriate methods for network analysis and promote the informed use of grouping methods in network research. The code used for these analyses has been made publicly available.

As a result, the typical effect that occurs when valleys are differently tilted is more accurately described as a change in the circular direction of motion, and is referred to as the orbital Hall effect.  This new understanding is demonstrated through both theoretical calculations and experiments, and is shown to differ only slightly from the original valley effect, allowing for a test of whether or not the orbital Hall effect is observable. In this paper, we explore the key concepts of minimal vertex sets within hypergraphs, introducing a measure of their density which is defined as the infimum of the real numbers for which each hypergraph's vertex set contains a subgraph meeting or exceeding this minimum density when comparing the size of the subgraph to the number of possible larger hypergraphs formed from it. An explicit expression is provided for the density of infinite hypergraphs in which every hypergraph has a finite number of vertices, as well as generalisations of theorems of Baker and Gloudeman. We demonstrate that the density of an infinite vertex set within a hypergraph need not necessarily equal the density of its largest subgraph, and that the density of infinite vertex sets can be distinct even within distinct hypergraphs sharing a common ground set. We also prove that the density of an infinite vertex set within a hypergraph defined through a function of two variables must be non-negative, and establish a sufficient condition under which the density of such a set within a hypergraph defined through a function of two variables is zero. In addition, further research into the determinants of minimal vertex sets and their relation to the geometry of hypergraphs is conducted, including an investigation into the possibility that a dense minimal vertex set within a hypergraph defined through a function of two variables must contain a plane defined by the points of three of its vertices. We find this to be false via construction, and that a minimal vertex set containing a plane defined by the points of three of its vertices may itself not be dense, as shown by an example illustrating this. We show, however, that the set of all vertices of a hypergraph defined through a function of two variables must be dense, as must the set formed by the closed balls of a fixed finite radius surrounding each of its vertices, and that these set collections encompass all dense vertex sets within such hypergraphs. We conclude our research with the proposal and resolution of a problem concerning the frequencies of odd and even numbers within a sequence defined by a polynomial of a single variable modulo $n$, and with the demonstration that a dense set of this sequence for a chosen natural number $n$ containing $n/2$ or more consecutive numbers must be one of the set collections described above. Furthermore, we show the sequence dense set criteria of 2 and $n/2$ also applies in the scenario in which $n$ is a square number. Ontologies are extensively utilized in various domains to define relationships between entities, yet they frequently encompass both hierarchical and non-hierarchical connections. Unfortunately, existing visualizations for ontologies tend to obscure the display of non-hierarchical links due to their focus on illustrating hierarchical structures. To address this, we present OntoPlot, a novel ontology visualization approach incorporating interactive visualization techniques. OntoPlot balances the display of all entities and connections, while also allowing users to seamlessly switch between non-hierarchical and hierarchical associations and investigate specific entities, including those without non-hierarchical links, to reveal hidden connections. Furthermore, OntoPlot incorporates a novel visualization method for hierarchical associations. We develop an ontology characterized by non-hierarchical links outweighing hierarchical ones and integrate OntoPlot into an existing tool widely employed for visualizing ontologies. Through OntoPlot's integration, users can effectively explore large, complex ontologies characterized by non-hierarchical links. We evaluate its performance using an ontology of US University Departments, a domain naturally comprising both hierarchical and non-hierarchical connections. OntoPlot's integration enables users to uncover previously unapparent university-level connections within individual colleges. Results from user testing, including positive feedback from domain experts, further affirm OntoPlot's utility in visualizing ontologies characterized by a mix of non-hierarchical and hierarchical connections. The implemented system, including OntoPlot, can be accessed online via a publicly accessible GitHub repository. Future work may involve enhancing OntoPlot's interaction capabilities to support computation of network centrality and other algorithms that are currently not directly integrated. The approach could also be extended to visualize datasets comprising non-hierarchical connections, even in cases where non-hierarchical links may be sparse. The accompanying video material documents OntoPlot's interaction and visualization capabilities. We introduce an innovative technique that leverages CycleGAN to bridge the gap between a speech model's original and synthesized audio formats, substantially improving speech recognition performance when limited labeled data is available. In addition to this, we find that incorporating speaker-independent training on English and Mandarin texts enhances the capabilities of the DeepSpeech library, and that cycle-consistency checking can significantly boost the system's effectiveness, particularly when a small set of auxiliary objectives, which we refer to as inter-domain losses, is incorporated. These auxiliary objectives, which include variants of the adversarial domain confusion loss, work to minimize the effect of the speaker's identity during training, thus preparing the model for speaker-variability. Furthermore, we investigate a range of inter-domain losses and evaluate their performance in various combinations. Through our experiments, we demonstrate that our novel method outperforms existing techniques, achieving a 20% reduction in word error rate on the EnglishSCO corpus and an impressive 11% reduction on the Librispeech corpus when limited to a small set of 400 hours of data. Notably, when our method is applied to a much larger dataset of 3000 hours, we observe a mere 1% decrease in word error rate compared to the standard DeepSpeech model. For deep neural networks to effectively utilize feedback, it's crucial that the agent generating predictions is part of an active prediction process. This research investigates the role of patient agents in a safe prediction framework. In the autonomous navigation of robots, patient agents receive non-exclusive predictions from local experts to avoid reliance on a single network. We demonstrate that our proposed safe prediction framework leads to improved safety and efficiency on real robotic scenarios. When incorporating uncertainty-based planning, our approach can reduce safety breaches by a significant 85%.6 Additionally, experimental results show that dividing predictions into levels can lower rates of safety breaches by up to 30% and increase on-average efficiency by 20%. We make our open-source code and documentation available.

The evaluation of student performance through written assignments spans multiple disciplines, yet relying solely on human assessment is impractical and costly. Automated methods are necessary to provide rapid, cost-effective feedback on student work. This research combines three approaches – surface-level, semantic-based, and translation-based evaluation – to assess automated systems' understanding. A dataset consisting of human marks and comprehensive error analyses for approximately 10,000 student essays was used to train a model that surpasses traditional BERT performance. This model outperformed human assessors in various evaluation methods, demonstrating exceptional accuracy while requiring only a tiny fraction of the computational resources. Interestingly, translation-based evaluation proved more effective than semantic-based evaluation. Further experiments involved fine-tuning different language models, including those based on both traditional and emerging transformer architectures, to optimize performance. While the most successful models utilized the translation-based approach, they required substantial computational resources. Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate how human observers perceive throwing actions where the ball is released abnormally, either before or after the optimal point of release. In astrophysics and astrochemistry, understanding how molecules form bonds with dust grains is crucial for interpreting observation data. Experimentally determining binding energies is often impractical, so theoretical calculations are utilized, yet these generate inconsistent results, necessitating a standardization in approaches for accurate inter-comparability. We present the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP), an online database containing a vast collection of theoretical binding energy data, employing a uniform analysis method to assess various approaches and informistances for calculating binding energies, particularly regarding full dehydrogenation and the deletion of hydrogen atoms. We utilize quantum Monte Carlo and density functional theory on silicate surfaces, as well as analysis methods like kT-distribution parameters and mean affinity weights. Our platform allows users to access analysis methods, associated data, visualizations of results, and comparisons with other's findings, supporting research into dust grain-solar molecule interactions in astrophysics and astrochemistry, as well as evaluations of hydrogen release mechanisms. We provide BEAP, a website containing the BEAP database, at https://beap.colorado.edu. Developing highly compact yet efficient NMT models is crucial, especially for low-resource machine translation scenarios. To achieve this, both quantization and distillation techniques have been effectively applied. While both methods aim to condense models, they utilize contrasting approaches: quantization physically alters the model while distillation modifies the model's behavior. As a result, distillation tends to produce more stable translations and is less susceptible to handling various types of data. Our study compares the stability of translation produced by applying quantization and distillation in a low-resource Arabic-English setting, emphasizing the need for techniques like distillation when developing compact yet robust NMT models. Moreover, we highlight the significance of a thorough evaluation of translation quality, especially for tasks involving rare names in low-resource scenarios. Our findings emphasize the value of additional training data in overcoming name translation difficulties. While quantization demonstrates some capacity to mitigate name translation issues through 'typos correction', it is distillation that yields notable improvements in BLEU scores (around +3). Additionally, by using BLEU scores as a proxy, we determine that distillation results in more consistent and stable translations across our entire dataset, as much as +10% improvement in METEOR metric on the entire dataset compared to quantization. Interestingly, using BLEU scores alone to evaluate both methods leads to a notable +5.8% METEOR improvement. Our analysis also reveals that utilizing both methods in conjunction, i.e., first distilling then quantizing the model, does not lead to additional gains, as combining them leads to some degradation (-1.1% METEOR). Artificial intelligence systems causing physical and financial harm necessitate direct examination, and incorporating causal analysis into AI development is recommended. An increasing number of financial applications utilize time series models, and we argue these systems are particularly vulnerable to causing harm if their causal components are overlooked. A novel metric, called "causal proxic harm," aims to quantify financial harm resulting from an AI's causal predictions in physically inherent environments. Calculating this metric involves complex pathways and intricate math, but concepts like causal value and proxic distance can simplify the process. By considering a financial institution's objectives, for example, the metric can be defined as the loss of a stock if a machine learns to predict damage to an institution's physical assets based on its financial performance. Such a metric enables operators to set boundaries on an AI's causal explanations for certain outcomes. An upcoming financial crisis dataset called the QuantCAD2 dataset will serve as a test case for evaluating this new metric. By examining how certain economic indicators like inflation and GDP affect breakdowns in time series models using QuantCAD2, a case is made for reorienting the sampling distribution in such financial contexts. By changing the sampling distribution in this way, an AI can avoid predicting certain causes of physical harm, thereby reducing harm resulting from its causal explanations. Thus, the paper recommends a new strategy for "soft boundary" supervision in financial applications, and future work will involve developing this supervision in real-time. Recent advancements in end-to-end speech-to-speech translation have been substantial but still fall short in two key areas: the need for extensive training data and a limited number of supported language pairs. This research addresses these two challenges by developing a framework for zero-shot speech-to-speech translation. Unlike conventional approaches, this system doesn't require training data for every possible language pair and instead uses a single training corpus for multiple language translations. However, this new framework also introduces the challenge of determining the target language from the input audio signal. This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing situations where a boundary's heat influx can fluctuate over time. To address this scenario efficiently, a mathematical framework involving the dual variables associated with the boundary conditions is developed, allowing for their derivation as part of an optimized control problem within a broader system. This optimization problem simulates the optimal thermal processing of a material without compromising its structural integrity. The ill-posedness of the resulting model is analyzed in detail, as well as the creation and characterization of a suitable solution space for the dual variable problem. An alternative approach to establishing uniqueness for the related problem of evolving boundary conditions is also presented and shown to be equivalent to the optimization perspective. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of the model is provided, encompassing situations where the boundary conditions are fixed or involve third-order nonlinear reactions, as well as an in-depth study of the model's behavior under various singular perturbation scenarios. The work culminates in the presentation of an asymptotic representation of the dual variable problem, accurate to the second-order, as part of a mathematical description of the model's behavior when the boundary conditions are fixed. The models and approaches described can be extended to address more complex situations, involving multiple space dimensions and dimensions akin to a graph. The work is grounded in the theoretical context of thermodynamics, ensuring that the proposed models are consistent with the associated entropy production principles. An extensive list of open problems is included at the conclusion of this dissertation. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disease. Manually identifying vertebrae in CT scans is time-consuming, so research has focused on semi-automated and automated methods. This paper introduces a novel, high-precision technique that uses spine rectification followed by anatomically-constrained optimization to accurately locate and identify vertebrae in lumbar CT scans, using minimal user input such as L1 and T1 vertebrae. This technique is unique in that it doesn't rely on complex segmentation or localization methods, but rather leverages spine curvature to automatically detect and align vertebrae. Once the spine is realigned, a conditional shape model is used to identify vertebrae. This technique was tested on 30 CT scans, yielding L1 to L5 vertebrae localization accuracy of mean absolute error 1.43 mm and 100% identification rate. In addition, it requires minimal user input, resulting in enhanced efficiency and adaptability. When applied to 200 CT scans, it achieved a mean absolute error of 1.67 mm and 100% identification rate. Compared to previous research using anatomically-constrained optimization, it demonstrates increased precision by an average of 0.47 mm. Experimental results also reveal that it outperforms semi-automated methods in terms of speed, requiring only 5-10 minutes to automatically identify and localize all lumbar vertebrae. This technique has the potential to greatly impact various medical applications related to spine disease. Further studies will focus on expanding this method to other types of imaging data and disease types. Through quantum electrodynamics, a complex interaction arises among the participating electrons, the core electron, and the surrounding photons in the cavity. This interaction results in the transfer of energy from the incoming electron to the core electron via a process of resonant scattering. On a timescale of 10's to 100s of attoseconds, a stable electron distribution emerges, sheltered from further radiation effects. This stable state provides a refuge for the core electron, shielding it from rapid radiation-driven transitions back to the ground state. The cavity's influence modulates the scattering rate and average electron energy according to its phase and amplitude variations. These modifications lead to an increased scattering probability and average energy when the cavity is in a particular phase, while opposite effects emerge when the cavity is in the opposing phase. This phenomenon exemplifies the dynamical stabilization of electronic states through the interplay of vacuum fluctuations and resonant interactions in an energetic scattering scenario. The presented findings may shed light on observed radiation effects in experiments and potentially reveal new phenomena in cavity-assisted scattering processes. The theoretical framework developed here can be applied to analyze and predict energy-dependent outcomes in electron and photon interactions within matter at the attosecond and femtosecond scale. Determining the depth of a scene in a light field consists of solving a complex problem, specifically decoding the complex geometry of the scene and overcoming occlusion, which are typically addressed separately. Most studies have emphasized improving the overall quality of the results without directly handling occlusion, resulting in estimated depths that are distorted by this issue. Others have introduced new modules to address occlusion, but often overlook the fact that their proposals still rely on existing weak local descriptors used elsewhere in the pipeline. In our proposal, we address both the overall issue and the distortion caused by occlusion by developing an innovative cost aggregation module. This new module is designed to prevent depth information from being shared between different points of view if there's occlusion between them, by using the structure across the views. We test the performance of our proposal on the established SAPIR dataset and find that our contribution leads to significant gains in accuracy, with results that suggest we're close to perfect accuracy on this dataset. Additionally, we create an even more advanced version of our proposal by integrating it with an efficient method for deciding the quality of different views and with a method for refining the results that uses information within the light field. We test these advancements on multiple datasets and find that our results match or surpass the results obtained using other methods for evaluating light field depth. Notably, our proposal allows us to achieve an accuracy score of 0.5763 on the SAPIR dataset, which is very close to the accuracy score achieved by the human eye in a similar evaluation. This study applies the bilinear method initially developed for shallow water equations by Fokas and other researchers, then extended to the Lenells equation. By using this approach, multiple soliton solutions are obtained, showcasing the system's integrability. Interestingly, employing the Fokas-Lenells equations requires noting a distinctive advection term. The resulting solutions display an intriguing interplay of oscillation and exponential decay. The obtained multi-soliton solutions yield a straightforward, step-by-step recursion for their coefficients. Notably, for two-soliton solutions, coefficients are entirely absent.
